title: Bidirectional catalysts with dual-atom dynamic d-band centre modulation and support self-reconstruction for de/hydrogenation in MgH_2/Mg

paper_content.abstract: High-capacity solid-state hydrogen storage using MgH2 requires high de/hydrogenation temperatures and exhibits sluggish kinetics. Although catalytic modification of MgH2 has been extensively studied, existing catalysts largely focus on unidirectional optimisation, failing to simultaneously and efficiently optimise the reversible hydrogen-storage properties of the MgH2/Mg system. Herein, we rationally design and construct a heteronuclear dual-atom catalyst, NiCo@TiO2. In this system, Ni and Co bidirectionally modulate the d-band centres, enabling synergistic and complementary catalysis. Specifically, Ni serves as the primary active site for Mg–H bond cleavage during dehydrogenation, facilitated by Co-induced d-band centre downshift. Conversely, Co acts as the primary active site for H2 dissociation during hydrogenation via Ni-triggered d-band centre upshift. Simultaneously, self-reconstruction of titanium species and oxygen vacancies, coupled with strong metal-support interactions (Ni/Co–TiO2), accelerate interfacial electron transfer and inhibit metal atom migration. This synergy significantly enhances both reaction kinetics and cycling stability, showing great promise for large-scale hydrogen-storage applications.
paper_content.introduction:
Hydrogen is an indispensable carbon-neutral energy carrier1–5, and its large-scale practical application mainly depends on two key factors: the safety of storage technologies and the enhancement of hydrogen storage density6–8. Solid-state hydrogen storage using magnesium hydride (MgH2) exhibits enhanced safety and high gravimetric density (7.6 wt.%); however, its practical deployment remains constrained by its sluggish de/hydrogenation kinetics requiring considerably high activation energies (dehydrogenation Ea > 160.0 kJ·mol−1, hydrogenation Ea > 87.3 kJ·mol−1)9–11. Several strategies, including alloying, nanoengineering, and catalyst addition, have been employed to overcome these challenges12–14. Reducing the kinetic barriers of de/hydrogenation in MgH2/Mg, particularly lowering the reaction temperatures and increasing the reaction rates, via catalytic engineering is the predominant strategy15–18.

Catalytic materials based on transition metals (e.g., Ni, Co, and Ti) and their oxides (e.g., TiO2) can considerably enhance the de/hydrogenation properties of MgH2/Mg owing to their unique d-orbital electronic structures14–22. Guan et al. developed a MgNi@Ti–MgO catalyst and incorporated it into MgH2 composites, reducing the initial dehydrogenation temperature to 172°C and leading to a dehydrogenation rate of 2.72 wt.%·min−1 H2 at 280°C20. AlMatrouk et al. calculated and revealed that Co-doped MgH2 shows considerably increased adsorption energy of H atoms on Mg surfaces compared to that of Ni atoms, lowering the energy barrier for hydrogen absorption21. However, the catalytic performance of these materials requires further optimisation to meet the stringent operating temperature constraints and reaction kinetic requirements for practical hydrogen fuel cell systems.

Single-atom catalysts (SACs), which are characterised by their maximal atomic utilisation, unique electronic structures, and precisely tuneable active sites, have demonstrated remarkable potential in different catalytic systems23–29. Previous work demonstrated that incorporating a specific single-atom catalyst into MgH2 significantly lowered the apparent activation energy (Ea) for both dehydrogenation and hydrogenation processes to 64.35 and 35.17 kJ·mol−1 H2, respectively30. However, the inherent mono-functionality of such catalysts often leads to an asymmetric catalytic profile27,28,31 which often means that catalysts excelling at dehydrogenation may perform suboptimally for hydrogenation. This kinetic disparity in the de/hydrogenation processes necessitates a rational design of bifunctional catalytic architectures. Heteronuclear dual-atom catalysts (DACs) can simultaneously and efficiently mediate two reaction pathways, and the synergistic effect of electron coupling and orbital hybridisation between bimetallic atoms may further improve the catalytic efficiency32–37. Given the established efficacy of Ni-based catalysts in promoting the dehydrogenation of MgH230, the selection of a complementary catalyst to optimise hydrogenation is critical.

Herein, we synthesised heteronuclear NiCo@TiO2 DACs using a hot molten salt method, leveraging complementary metal synergies to enable the bidirectional regulation of the de/hydrogenation processes in MgH2/Mg systems. Ni and Co atoms synergistically form active centres with complementary roles on MgH2/Mg. During dehydrogenation, Ni serves as the principal site for Mg–H bond cleavage, while Co modulates Ni’s d-band centre to reduce Mg–H bond energy. Conversely, during hydrogenation, Co dominates H2 dissociation, with Ni optimising Co’s d-band centre to facilitate hydrogen adsorption. Concurrently, self-reconstruction of multivalent titanium species (Tix+) and oxygen vacancies (OV) within the TiO2 support and strong metal-support interactions (Ni/Co–TiO2) effectively promote interfacial electron transfer and suppress metal atom migration, remarkably enhancing reaction kinetics and cycling stability. Specifically, the ball-milled NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 composite achieved a low initial dehydrogenation temperature (168°C), with an accelerated initial hydrogen desorption rate of 3.02 wt.%·min−1 at 275°C, while enabling efficient room-temperature hydrogen absorption (3.79 wt.% within 30 min at 30°C). The system exhibited outstanding kinetics, showing low Ea for desorption (Ea,de = 53.54 kJ·mol−1) and absorption (Ea,ab = 16.71 kJ·mol−1), and maintained 97.6% capacity retention over 100 de/hydrogenation cycles. This work enhanced hydrogen storage performances in MgH2-based systems while proposing a universal design framework for reversible chemical processes.
paper_content.results:
Theoretical design of catalysts
To overcome the kinetic limitations of the de/hydrogenation processes in MgH2/Mg systems, a dual-atom catalytic strategy was employed. The selection of Ni-Co dual-atom sites was motivated by their complementary electronic configurations: Ni’s d8 orbital occupancy enables moderate hydrogen binding strength, facilitating H2 release, while Co’s high-spin d7 state promotes low-barrier H2 dissociation via enhanced σ* orbital back-donation38–42. Concurrently, TiO2 was selected as the support owing to its intrinsic defect-tunable nature (facile oxygen vacancy formation) and reversible redox activity43–45. Moreover, the synergistic metal-metal interactions (Ni–Co) and strong metal-support interaction (SMSI) between reducible oxide supports (TiO2) and loaded metals (Ni/Co) under elevated temperatures can effectively facilitate interfacial charge transfer and enhance cycling stability during the de/hydrogenation cycles of MgH2/Mg systems46–49.

Building upon the preceding literature analysis on atom and support, we further perform theoretical calculations to evaluate the catalytic superiority of the NiCo@TiO2 DACs for hydrogen storage in the MgH2/Mg system, thereby guiding subsequent experimental studies. The Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package was used to develop theoretical models of five dehydrogenation systems: pure MgH2, TiO2–MgH2, Ni@TiO2–MgH2, Co@TiO2–MgH2, and NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 (Supplementary Fig. 1). The theoretical models utilized the anatase TiO2 (101) surface, which is the most stable and predominantly exposed facet, as confirmed by subsequent experimental characterization. Having established the rationality of the model and the stability of the catalyst via the binding and migration energy barriers of Ni/Co atoms on the TiO2 support (Supplementary Fig. 2; also confirmed by the following experiment characterizations), we further employed Density functional theory (DFT) calculations to systematically investigate the electronic coupling between Ni and Co atoms during the de/hydrogenation processes of MgH2/Mg systems. And all calculations were performed under these well-established and rigorously tested settings (Supplementary Fig. 3 and Table 1).

The dehydrogenation process in MgH2/Mg systems was quantitatively evaluated by studying Mg–H bond-strength variations in different catalytic environments. Crystal orbital Hamilton population (COHP) analysis revealed that the combination of different catalysts with MgH2 lead to the weakening of bonding orbitals near the Fermi level of MgH2 (Supplementary Fig. 4). The order of the integrated COHP (-ICOHP) values was as follows: NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 (0.22 eV) < Ni@TiO2–MgH2 (0.41 eV) < Co@TiO2–MgH2 (0.45 eV) < TiO2–MgH2 (0.91 eV) < pure MgH2 (0.95 eV); lower -ICOHP values indicate weaker Mg–H bonding interactions (Fig. 1a). The SACs lead to significant bond weakening, reducing the Mg–H bond strength by 56.84% (Ni@TiO2) and 52.63% (Co@TiO2) compared to that in pure MgH2. Furthermore, the dual-atom system achieved a 76.84% bond-strength reduction through non-linear synergy, suggesting that the Ni/Co dual sites worked together to significantly decrease the Mg–H bond energy, enhancing the dehydrogenation performance of MgH2. In addition, to compare the catalytic effects of the OV-rich and Tix+-rich TiO2 support with those of Ni/Co atoms on MgH2, the -ICOHP values of pure MgH2, TiO2–MgH2, TiO2–OV–MgH2 and NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 were further compared, revealing the predominant catalytic role of Ni/Co atoms in governing dehydrogenation kinetics (Supplementary Fig. 5).

To investigate the catalytic mechanism of NiCo@TiO2 DACs in MgH2 dehydrogenation, a partial density of states (PDOS) analysis was performed. The strong electronic coupling between Ni and Co atoms in NiCo@TiO2 is illustrated in Fig. 1b and c, illustrating that Ni 3d and Co 3d exhibited substantial density of states (DOS) values within the energy range from −4 to 2 eV. The d-band centre of Ni in NiCo@TiO2 shifted downwards to −1.806 eV compared to −1.363 eV in Ni@TiO2. Conversely, the d-band centre of Co shifted upwards from −1.907 eV (Co@TiO2) to −1.774 eV (NiCo@TiO2). The dynamic d-band centre modulation enabled Ni and Co atoms to function as complementary active sites for de/hydrogenation, respectively, suggesting a possibility for achieving bidirectional catalysis in MgH2/Mg systems.

The PDOS of the s orbitals of the H atoms, as well as those of the s and p orbitals of the Mg atoms near the Fermi level decreased (Supplementary Fig. 6), suggesting a decrease in the orbital energy of the H and Mg atoms, which indicated a weakening of the Mg–H bond strength. The PDOS peaks of H and Mg in NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 exhibited the lowest overlap and intensity, which is in good agreement with the COHP analysis results, indicating that this composite had the lowest Mg–H bond strength.

Next, the dissociation of hydrogen molecules was systematically investigated under various catalytic conditions to evaluate the effect of the catalysts on hydrogen absorption. As illustrated in Fig. 1d, the introduction of the SACs and DACs considerably reduced the energy barrier for hydrogen dissociation. Comparative analysis revealed that Co@TiO2–Mg had a lower hydrogen dissociation energy barrier (ΔE = 0.384 eV) compared to Ni@TiO2–Mg (ΔE = 0.415 eV), indicating that Co@TiO2 showed an enhanced capability to destabilise H–H bonds and facilitate the dissociation of H2 into atomic hydrogen. NiCo@TiO2–Mg demonstrated the lowest energy barrier for hydrogen dissociation (ΔE = 0.193 eV), which was attributed to the synergistic interaction between Ni and Co. This synergistic effect increased the kinetics of H2 dissociation and substantially enhanced the overall hydrogen absorption performance of the MgH2/Mg hydrogen storage system.

Collectively, the synergy of Ni–Co triggers a downward shift in the d-band centre of Ni and an upward shift in Co. Specifically, the downward shift of the d-band centre of Ni reduced the orbital overlap between the Ni 3d and H 1s orbitals, reducing the Ni–H adsorption strength. This electronic modification facilitated hydrogen atom diffusion throughout the catalytic system. In contrast, the upward shift of the d-band centre of Co strengthened the interactions between the Co 3d orbitals and H2 molecules. This optimised the binding strength of H2 molecules adsorbed on the Co sites and promoted H2 dissociation by enhancing the hybridisation of Co 3d with H2 σ* orbitals, allowing efficient H migration to the Mg surface for MgH2 formation. Thus, Ni and Co atoms in NiCo@TiO2 DACs can achieve efficient bidirectional catalysis in MgH2/Mg systems, facilitating the rational design and experimental development of DACs.

Synthesis and microstructure of NiCo@TiO2 DACs
Driven by DFT calculations revealing the significant enhancement of MgH2/Mg hydrogen storage performance by the DACs, we strategically designed and synthesised the dual-atom Ni and Co supported on TiO2 with three precisely controlled Ni/Co atomic ratios (7:3, 1:1, and 3:7) via a hot molten salt method. The successful incorporation and precise quantification of Ni and Co in the catalysts were verified by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). The Ni/Co atomic ratios were controlled by adjusting the precursor concentrations (Supplementary Table 2) and were measured to be 2.13, 0.96, and 0.45, demonstrating the tunability of the synthesis method. NiCo@TiO2 (Ni/Co atomic ratio determined by ICP-MS = 0.96) exhibited the best catalytic performance in enhancing the hydrogen storage properties of MgH2, as evidenced by comprehensive evaluation. Thus, it was selected for subsequent in-depth characterisation.

The phase structure of the synthesised sample was characterised by X-ray diffraction (XRD). The results indicated three strong diffraction peaks at 2θ = 25.3°, 38.2°, and 48.2°, which highly matched the standard spectra of the TiO2 anatase phase (Fig. 2a). No diffraction peaks attributed to Ni and Co were detected in the XRD pattern, which preliminarily suggested that Ni and Co coexisted in an amorphous phase or a single-atom form.

To directly reveal the dispersion state of Ni and Co on TiO2, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) were used. The catalyst exhibited uniform morphology with particle sizes of 40–60 nm (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 7). High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) analysis revealed a lattice spacing of 0.3520 nm (Fig. 2c), corresponding to the (101) plane of anatase TiO2. A detailed selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern showed ordered diffraction rings with d-spacings of 0.3520 and 0.1892 nm (Fig. 2d), corresponding to the (101) and (200) planes of anatase TiO2, respectively. These results were in good agreement with the XRD patterns, revealing the core structural characteristics of NiCo@TiO2, i.e., the main body is a highly crystallised TiO2 anatase phase.

The high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM, Fig. 2e) revealed bright spots uniformly distributed across the TiO2 substrate. Given the higher atomic masses of Ni and Co compared to those of Ti, these bright spots were attributed to the dual-atom sites (marked by green circles) and a few single-atom sites. Statistical analysis of the measured atomic spacing yielded an average Ni-Co distance of 0.247 nm (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Fig. 8). Moreover, the Ni/Co atomic intensities possess higher intensity than the Ti atomic intensity based on the HAADF-STEM analysis of the NiCo@TiO2 DACs (Fig. 2g). Further, the HAADF-STEM via electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) clearly reveals the presence of Co and Ni, confirming the Co−Ni dual-atom pairs in NiCo@TiO2 DACs (Fig. 2h). The energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) elemental mapping (Fig. 2i) confirmed the presence of both metals, suggesting the successful incorporation of Ni and Co species with high dispersion on the TiO2 support. Thus, the synthesised catalyst consisted of mono-dispersed Ni and Co atoms uniformly distributed on the TiO2 substrate. For reference and comparison, the microstructures of corresponding Ni@TiO2 and Co@TiO2 SACs are provided in the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Figs. 9 and 10).

Further, X-ray absorption spectroscopy was employed to precisely determine the local geometric structures of Ni and Co at the atomic level. Figure 3a and b shows the Ni and Co K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra for NiCo@TiO2, alongside the corresponding reference spectra from metal foils (Ni, Co), oxides (NiO, CoO, Co3O4), and single-atom catalysts (Ni@TiO2, Co@TiO2). Specifically, the Ni K-edge XANES spectrum of NiCo@TiO2 was considerably different from those of the Ni foil and NiO, which further reflected the unique state of Ni in the catalyst. Moreover, the absorption edge energy of NiCo@TiO2 was higher than that of the Ni foil and Ni@TiO2 and lower than that of NiO, indicating that the valency of Ni species in NiCo@TiO2 was between 0 and +2, slightly higher than that of Ni species in Ni@TiO2. According to the Co K-edge XANES spectrum of NiCo@TiO2, the valency of Co species in NiCo@TiO2 is higher than that of Co@TiO2 (Fig. 3b). The observed intermediate valence states of Ni and Co originate from the strong metal-support interaction (SMSI) with the TiO2 support. This interaction causes partial charge transfer, resulting in electronic structures that are intermediate between their metallic and oxidized states, which are distinct from the mere physical mixture25,50–53.

More detailed atomic structure information was obtained using the k2-weighted Fourier transform (FT) extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) of Ni and Co K-edge in the R space. The characteristic peaks of the Ni–Ni bond in the Ni foil and Co–Co bonds in the Co foil were located at 2.16 and 2.18 Å, respectively (Fig. 3c and d), which were absent in the NiCo@TiO2, proving that Ni and Co atoms achieved atomic dispersion on TiO2 rather than forming metal clusters or particles. Moreover, the peaks of Ni and Co in the R space of NiCo@TiO2 at 1.75 and 1.53 Å were attributed to the first coordination shell of Ni–O and Co–O bonds (Fig. 3c and 3d), respectively.

To further analyse the coordination states of Ni and Co, their wavelet-transformed (WT) K-edge EXAFS oscillations were studied. As shown in Fig. 3e and f, the strongest oscillations of NiCo@TiO2 appeared around the wave vector of 5 Å−1, which was close to the wave vectors pertaining to the strongest oscillations of NiO and CoO. The backscattered atoms bonded with Ni and Co were O atoms. To further identify the fine coordination configurations of Ni and Co in different samples, quantitative least squares EXAFS curve-fitting analyses were conducted (Fig. 3g, h and Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12). The analysis revealed distinct coordination environments in NiCo@TiO2, with Ni–O and Co–O coordination numbers of 4.9 and 5.1, respectively (Supplementary Table 3). The Ni–O coordination number in NiCo@TiO2 (4.9) was considerably higher than that in Ni@TiO2 SACs (4.3). Conversely, the Co–O coordination number (5.1) was lower than that in Co@TiO2 SACs (5.4). Based on the characterisation results, the coordination environment of isolated Ni and Co atoms on the TiO2 support can be determined (Fig. 3g, h). This altered coordination condition suggested potential electronic interactions between Ni and Co, which may have a positive effect on promoting efficient electron transfer during the de/hydrogenation process of MgH2/Mg systems.

These characterisations demonstrated the atomic dispersion of Ni and Co in NiCo@TiO2. This atomic-level structural elucidation provides a fundamental basis for understanding the enhanced catalytic properties and exploring the potential applications of this dual-atom catalyst system.

Fabrication and dispersion of NiCo@TiO2 DACs on MgH2
Through systematic optimisation of ball-milling parameters, the as-synthesised NiCo@TiO2 DACs were uniformly dispersed on MgH2 surfaces, forming homogeneous composites. XRD analysis confirmed the β-MgH2 phase in composites, with characteristic peaks at 27.9°, 35.7°, and 39.85° corresponding to the (110), (111), and (200) crystal planes, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 13). The distinct broadening of the MgH2 peak indicated its reduced crystallite size (based on Scherrer analysis) and lattice strain induced by mechanical milling, which are structural modifications known to enhance hydrogen diffusion kinetics. The low-intensity peak at 25.3° corresponded to the (101) plane of the TiO2 anatase phase.

SEM images and corresponding EDS mapping reveal that the surface of MgH2 particles (∼8 μm) is uniformly decorated with NiCo@TiO2 DACs (Supplementary Fig. 14). Furthermore, the spatial distribution of NiCo@TiO2 DACs and their coherent boundary with MgH2 were explored using TEM at various scales (Fig. 4a, b). HRTEM images also revealed close interfacial contact between the catalysts and the MgH2 matrix (Fig. 4c). The measured interplanar spacings of 0.2512 and 0.1890 nm corresponded to the (101) plane of β-MgH2 and (200) plane of TiO2 anatase, respectively. This nanoscale integration created coherent phase boundaries that likely generated preferential pathways for hydrogen transport54,55. SAED patterns (Fig. 4d) further confirmed the nature of the composite, displaying concentric rings indexed to the TiO2 (101), MgH2 (101), MgO (200), and TiO2 (200) planes. The presence of MgO (d = 0.2110 nm) may be attributed to surface oxidation during the test.

The elemental distribution was studied based on atomic-scale characterisation using HAADF-STEM (Fig. 4e) coupled with EDS mapping (Fig. 4f). Isolated bright spots with Z-contrast differences confirmed the atomic dispersion of Ni/Co species within the TiO2 lattice. Dual-atom sites (marked by green circles) and a few single-atom sites were observed, indicating that Ni and Co atoms still maintained the atomic-level dispersed state in the composite sample. Elemental mapping results indicated a homogeneous spatial distribution of Ti, Ni, Co, O, and Mg throughout the composite. Thus, atomically dispersed Ni–Co dual-metal sites anchored on the TiO2 support were uniformly distributed within the MgH2 matrix, providing abundant interfaces for catalysing hydrogen storage.

The comprehensive characterisation revealed the successful fabrication of structurally integrated NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 composites. The precisely designed interface architecture, featuring a reduced MgH2 crystallite size and atomically dispersed transition metals on TiO2, provides an ideal platform for catalysing hydrogen storage and investigating mechanisms in subsequent research.

Hydrogen storage property of MgH2/Mg with various catalysts
To systematically investigate the catalytic effect of NiCo@TiO2 DACs on the hydrogen desorption properties of MgH2, we conducted temperature-programmed desorption (TPD) measurements (Fig. 5a). The 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 composite exhibited a considerably low initial desorption temperature of 168°C, representing a substantial reduction of 212°C compared to that of pure MgH2, and a hydrogen storage capacity of 6.49 wt.%. The catalytic efficiency of the 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 composite surpassed those of Ni@TiO2 and Co@TiO2 SACs under identical conditions. Mass spectrometry analysis revealed that the dehydrogenation peak temperature of 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 was 220°C (Fig. 5a inset).

Additionally, previous studies have shown that V2O5 and Nb2O5 exhibit good catalytic performance for MgH256–60. Therefore, we used V2O5 and Nb2O5 as supports to prepare the dual-atom catalysts NiCo@V2O5 and NiCo@Nb2O5, which were then combined with MgH2 using the same method. Compared with 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2, both 15 wt.%-NiCo@V2O5–MgH2 and 15 wt.%-NiCo@Nb2O5–MgH2 have higher dehydrogenation temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 15), demonstrating the advantage of using TiO2 as the support. Furthermore, we have discovered that the oxygen vacancy (OV) concentration of TiO2 support exhibits a volcano-like dependency on the catalytic performance in the MgH2/Mg systems (Supplementary Fig. 16). This peak performance could be attributed to an optimal density of active sites, which provides a high concentration of vacancies for hydrogen adsorption and dissociation while maintaining their dispersion and stability61–64. Accordingly, the preparation of DACs can involve maintaining the OV concentration within an optimal range.

To further elucidate the effect of the atomic composition on the catalytic activity, DACs with different Ni/Co ratios (Ni0.3Co0.7@TiO2, NiCo@TiO2, and Ni0.7Co0.3@TiO2) were designed, and their TPD profiles were evaluated (Supplementary Fig. 17). Among them, NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 demonstrated superior dehydrogenation performance. Ni0.3Co0.7@TiO2–MgH2 and Ni0.7Co0.3@TiO2–MgH2 exhibited enhanced hydrogen storage properties compared to their monatomic counterparts, highlighting the synergistic catalytic effect between the two metals. MgH2 with different NiCo@TiO2 concentrations (10, 15, and 20 wt.%) was prepared to optimise the catalyst loading through ball milling. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 18, the 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 was the optimal catalyst for hydrogen storage applications, as it demonstrated the optimal dehydrogenation temperature, rate, and capacity.

The isothermal desorption properties of 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 were further investigated at 275°C, 250°C, 225°C and 200°C (Fig. 5b). At 275°C, 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 released over 5.91 wt.% H2 within 4 min, exhibiting excellent dehydrogenation kinetics. As the temperature decreased, the kinetics of dehydrogenation slightly decreased. Even at 200 °C, 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 still released 2.31 wt.% H2 in 20 min and eventually released > 4.42 wt.% of H2 within 180 min (Supplementary Fig. 19). The observation of a slight sigmoidal shape in isothermal dehydrogenation curves, particularly at lower temperatures, is characteristic of a reaction controlled by the nucleation and growth of Mg65–67. The brief induction period arises from the energy barrier to form critical Mg nuclei, which is rapidly overcome at elevated temperatures, thereby leading to near-linear kinetics. Moreover, SEM images of the dehydrogenated 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 sample at 275°C reveal a uniform distribution of the NiCo@TiO2 DACs on the Mg surface (Supplementary Fig. 20), confirming excellent structural stability.

Figure 5c shows the isothermal hydrogenation kinetics of 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–Mg, i.e., dehydrogenated 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2, under a hydrogen pressure of 40 bar. The 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–Mg composite absorbed 4.67 wt.% at 50°C within 30 min. Based on the superior hydrogenation kinetics, the hydrogenation kinetics at room temperature (30 °C) were further tested, revealing that 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–Mg absorbed 3.79 wt.% and 5.47 wt.% H2 within 30 and 600 min (Supplementary Fig. 21a), respectively, demonstrating excellent hydrogen absorption kinetics. To obtain faster hydrogen adsorption and higher capacity, we investigated the hydrogenation behaviour of 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–Mg at higher temperatures, which absorbed 6.32 wt.% H2 within 20 s at 250°C (Supplementary Fig. 21b), demonstrating a high hydrogen absorption rate and near-saturation capacity.

The desorption/absorption apparent Ea is a crucial parameter for characterizing the de/hydrogenation kinetics. The dehydrogenation kinetics were evaluated by applying nine distinct kinetic models (Supplementary Table 4). According to the fitting results (Supplementary Fig. 22), the R3 model (three-dimensional phase boundary) exhibited the best agreement with the experimental data at 275°C, as indicated by a slope nearest to unity. The applicability of the R3 model suggests that the dehydrogenation process is controlled by a three-dimensional growth of Mg nuclei at the phase interface, indicating that NiCo@TiO2 DACs could increase the nucleation sites of Mg by promoting the diffusion of hydrogen68,69. The desorption Ea was derived from the linear fitting of lnk and 1000/T (Fig. 5d), yielding a value of 53.54 kJ·mol−1, which corresponds to a 66.5% reduction compared to pure MgH2. Similarly, the Ea for hydrogenation was calculated to be 16.71 kJ·mol−1, representing a decrease of 72.2%.

The thermodynamics were further probed through Pressure-Composition-Temperature measurement (Supplementary Fig. 23). The derived dehydrogenation enthalpy (ΔH) of 71.67 kJ·mol−1 H2 is lower than that of pure MgH2 (76.41 kJ·mol−1 H2), confirming that the NiCo@TiO2 DACs not only improve the kinetics but also decrease thermodynamics stability of the hydrogen storage process in MgH2/Mg systems, which is consistent with our DFT calculations.

To evaluate the practical application potential of 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2, its reversible cycle performance was investigated in depth. Isothermal H2 absorption and desorption were conducted at 280°C (Fig. 5e). Even after 100 cycles, the catalysed MgH2/Mg retained 97.6% of its capacity, demonstrating excellent cycle stability. The SEM and HAADF-STEM characterisations combined with the corresponding EDS elemental mapping of the 100-cycled sample revealed that the atomic-scale distribution of individual metal atoms and the dispersion of the NiCo@TiO2 DACs on the MgH2 surface remained highly uniform (Supplementary Figs. 24–25). The excellent stability of the sample can be attributed to the enhanced interfacial electron transfer enabled by the metal–metal (Ni–Co) interactions, while the strong metal–support (Ni/Co–TiO2) interactions effectively suppress metal atom migration47,70. Furthermore, the XRD patterns revealed negligible peak shift between the pristine and the 100-cycled sample, indicating excellent structural consistency. However, the pattern of the 100-cycled sample showed intensified peaks and a reduced full width at half maximum for MgH2 (Supplementary Fig. 26), suggesting increased crystallinity and grain coarsening during cycling, which may account for the observed slight capacity degradation. Overall, this structural integrity strongly supports the robust reversibility and exceptional cyclic stability of the NiCo@TiO2 DAC-catalysed MgH2/Mg systems, underscoring its practical suitability for hydrogen storage applications.

To comprehensively evaluate the superior catalytic performance of the NiCo@TiO2 DACs in the MgH2 hydrogen storage system, we systematically compared their catalytic effects with those of nano-catalysts (NiNP@TiO2, CoNP@TiO2, and NiCoNP@TiO2) and SACs (Ni@TiO2 and Co@TiO2) under identical conditions. Unlike those of the SACs and DACs, the XRD patterns of the nano-catalysts exhibited distinct peaks corresponding to metallic Ni and Co phases (Supplementary Fig. 27), confirming the successful deposition of Ni/Co nanoparticles on the TiO2 support. This was confirmed by the presence of characteristic lattice fringes associated with Ni and Co in the HRTEM images (Supplementary Figs. 28–30), confirming nanoparticle formation.

The TPD analysis of the composites of MgH2 with different catalysts (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 31) revealed that the composites corresponding to nano-catalysts exhibited high dehydrogenation temperatures and sluggish desorption kinetics compared to the SACs and DACs, highlighting the key role of atomic-scale catalytic design in optimising the hydrogen release properties. Furthermore, the Ni-based catalysts (NiNP@TiO2 and Ni@TiO2) led to substantially lower peak desorption temperatures for MgH2 than Co-based catalysts (CoNP@TiO2 and Co@TiO2), indicating more pronounced improvements in the hydrogen release properties (Fig. 5f). The Ni–Co synergistic effect (NiCoNP@TiO2 and NiCo@TiO2) can further reduce the initial and peak dehydrogenation temperatures of MgH2.

Subsequently, we conducted a comprehensive comparative analysis of the average de/hydrogenation rates and the corresponding Ea of MgH2 under isothermal conditions for six distinct catalytic systems (Supplementary Figs. 32–36). Similarly, the Ni-based catalyst substantially enhanced the dehydrogenation process in MgH2/Mg, whereas the Co-based catalyst exhibited better performance in hydrogen absorption. Furthermore, the Ni–Co synergistic interactions simultaneously improved the hydrogen absorption and desorption processes in MgH2/Mg. The NiCo@TiO2 DACs–catalysed MgH2/Mg achieved the fastest reaction kinetics and the lowest Ea barrier. The kinetic analysis revealed that 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 achieved a remarkable hydrogen desorption rate (3.02 wt.%·min−1) at 275°C and a near-room-temperature hydrogen absorption rate (0.73 wt.%·min−1) at 50°C (Fig. 5g). The lowest Ea for the hydrogen absorption and desorption in MgH2/Mg under six catalytic conditions further highlight the exceptional capability of NiCo@TiO2 DACs in promoting the Mg–H bonds breaking and reducing the H2 dissociation barrier (Fig. 5h), indicating their superiority in hydrogen storage applications (Supplementary Table 5).

Previous reports have indicated that the elements Pd/Ru exhibit extremely excellent catalytic effects on the MgH2/Mg systems56,71,72. Given these established findings and the promising catalytic performance of Ni and Co observed in our study, we conducted additional TPD experiments to directly compare the hydrogen desorption behaviour of the NiCo@TiO2 DACs with several reference catalysts. These included single-atom catalysts (Ru@TiO2, Pd@TiO2) and other dual-atom systems (such as RuCo@TiO2, RuNi@TiO2, PdNi@TiO2, PdRu@TiO2, PdCo@TiO2). All catalysts were synthesized and tested under identical conditions. The TPD curves (Supplementary Fig. 37) clearly demonstrate that MgH2 catalysed by NiCo@TiO2 DACs achieves the lowest initial and peak desorption temperatures among all tested SACs and DACs. Furthermore, compared to systems reported in previous studies (Supplementary Table 6), 15 wt.%-NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 exhibits superior performance in terms of reduced dehydrogenation temperature, enhanced dehydrogenation rate, as well as decreased activation energy and enthalpy. This exceptional performance highlights that the synergy in NiCo@TiO2 DACs is not merely a generic diatomic effect, but rather a unique electronic cooperation between Ni/Co atoms and TiO2 support.

Catalysis mechanism in NiCo@TiO2–MgH2 systems
Building upon the DFT-calculated mechanism insights in the first section, experimental characterisation was employed to further study the catalytic mechanism of NiCo@TiO2 DACs for hydrogen storage. XPS characterisation reveals a systematic decrease in the value of OL (oxygen lattice)/OV in all samples from 85/15 (pristine TiO2) to 76/24 (NiCo@TiO2), 34/66 (ball-milled composite) and 27/73 (dehydrogenated sample), indicating the gradual increase in the OV concentrations (Fig. 6a). The OV content in the hydrogenation sample decreased compared to that in the dehydrogenated sample, returning to the level observed in the ball-milled sample, which reveals the reversible evolution and self-reconstruction of the catalyst during de/hydrogenation cycles.

These quantitative results also demonstrate significant variations in polyvalent Tix+ species among different samples. The detailed deconvolution of Ti 2p spectra revealed that the change in the Ti valence state is strongly correlated with the OV concentration (Fig. 6b and Supplementary Table 7). Complementary XRD analysis (Supplementary Fig. 26) of the first dehydrogenation products showed only the peaks of the Mg and TiO2 composites. This disappearance of the TiO2 phase confirms the Tix+ and OV evolutions. Moreover, it can be clearly observed that introducing dispersed atoms and using ball milling effectively increases the OV content, as indicated by the XPS results. The increased OV serves as an active site, improving electron transport, whereas the Tix+ species act as crucial intermediates during the electron transfer between Mg2+ and H−73–75.

To elucidate the electronic synergy between the Ni/Co dual-atom sites and the TiO2 support at the nanoscale, atomic force microscopy (AFM) and Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) were used to quantitatively map the surface potential distribution in pure TiO2, Co@TiO2, Ni@TiO2, and NiCo@TiO2. High-resolution AFM images (Fig. 6c) show TiO2 nanoparticles (diameter = 40–60 nm) with homogeneous dispersion, while KPFM mapping (Fig. 6d) shows pronounced surface potential difference at the nanoscale. Statistical analysis of surface potentials demonstrated that the substantial potential contrast of NiCo@TiO2 DACs (median value = 34.47 mV), representing 71.07% and 105.79% enhancements over Ni@TiO2 SACs (median value = 20.15 mV) and Co@TiO2 SACs (median value = 16.75 mV), respectively (Fig. 6e). The higher surface potential difference in NiCo@TiO2 indicates a lower work function. According to the definition of work function (Eq. 1), the reduced work function corresponds to an upward shift of the Fermi level, enhancing their electron-donating capacity.

Φ = EV − EF, (1)

where EV is the vacuum level (EV = 0) and EF is the Fermi level. Furthermore, the elevated Fermi level reduces the desorption energy barrier of H− in MgH2 and accelerates the dehydrogenation kinetics via a Tix+-mediated electron-transfer pathway, ultimately enhancing the catalytic activity of NiCo@TiO2 DACs18. Thus, the NiCo@TiO2 DACs’ superior catalytic performance compared to SACs can be attributed to the optimised electronic structure of NiCo@TiO2 DACs, which facilitates the charge transfer during the de/hydrogenation cycles of MgH2.

Based on the above experimental and computational results, a comprehensive mechanism for the de/hydrogenation processes was proposed (Fig. 6f). The core of the hydrogen desorption process is breaking the Mg–H bonds. The dehydrogenation process is elucidated in the following points. (1) The introduction of Ni and Co atoms into the MgH2/Mg hydrogen storage system disrupts the Mg–H bonding orbitals, generating anti-bonding states near the Fermi level, weakening the Mg–H bond energy. (2) Ni exhibits superior catalytic activity over Co, and Ni serves as the primary active site. Driven by Co-induced electronic coupling, the downward shift of Ni’s d-band centre precisely modulates Mg–H bond weakening, concertedly reducing bond dissociation energy and facilitating Mg nucleation. (3) The TiO2 support, which is present as polyvalent Tix+ in NiCo@TiO2 DACs, serves as an effective electron-transfer medium due to its mixed-valence characteristics, which were confirmed by the transformation of most high-valent Ti to low-valent Ti after dehydrogenation. (4) The synergistic effect of Ni/Co dual-site considerably enhances the electron-transfer capability of TiO2, facilitating the migration of electrons from H− to Tix+ and then to Mg2+, lowering the energy for breaking the Mg–H bonds and promoting Mg nucleation.

H2 molecule dissociation is the main factor for hydrogen absorption process. The hydrogenation process can be elucidated in the following steps. (1) The synergistic coupling of Ni and Co atoms enables dynamic modulation of the d-band centre. Specifically, Ni induces an upward shift in the d-band centre of Co atoms to enhance hydrogen adsorption. (2) The increased d-band centre of Co enables efficient H2 dissociation and enhanced hydrogen atom diffusion, establishing Co as the primary active site for H2 activation within the Mg hydrogenation system. (3) The TiO2 support maintains a polyvalent valence state (predominantly in low oxidation states) in the dehydrogenation product, functioning as an electron-transfer mediator in the process of hydrogenation to enable catalytic electron cycling, which was confirmed by the reversible transformation of Ti from a low oxidation state to a high oxidation state, indicating the self-reconstruction of the support during de/hydrogenation cycling. (4) The Ni/Co dual-site exhibits a synergistic effect that markedly enhances the electron-transfer capability of TiO2, promoting efficient electron migration from Mg to Tix+ and subsequently to H2.

In summary, the superior catalytic performance of NiCo@TiO2 DACs is attributed to a concerted mechanism orchestrated by Ni/Co atoms and the TiO2 support. (1) Dual-atom synergy: The Ni-Co heteronuclear dual-atom catalyst features complementary electronic and orbital properties, which enhance de/hydrogenation by optimising the d-band centres of both metals and lowering energy barriers for Mg–H bond cleavage and H2 dissociation. During dehydrogenation, Ni acts as the principal site for Mg–H bond cleavage, while Co modulates the d-band centre of Ni to further weaken the Mg–H bond energy. In hydrogenation, Co serves as the dominant site for H–H bond dissociation, whereas Ni optimises the d-band centre of Co, shifting it upwards to facilitate hydrogen adsorption and dissociation. (2) TiO2 support function: TiO2 support undergoes self-reconstruction throughout the reversible de/hydrogenation processes, contributing to the catalytic functionality and stability. (3) Metal–support interaction: Dual-atom Ni/Co promotes the generation of OV and polyvalent Ti in the TiO2 support, OV as the active site accelerates the electron transport, and the Ti as an intermediate for electron transport, passing the electron and presenting valence change, which avoids the high bond energy caused by the direct breaking of the Mg-H bond. Concurrently, the interface formed between isolated Ni/Co atoms and Tix+ species creates atomically dispersed Ni/Co–O–Tix+ active centres, which further enhance catalytic activity.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript from Jinlong Jin, Jiyue Zhang, Jingjing Zhang, Xiaowei Chen, Heyi Qian, Bohua Jia, Jinghua Liu, Baoxin Han, Wentao Wang, Xiaojun Yan,, Jianglan Shui, and Jianmei Huang reports on the use of heteronuclear dual-atom catalysts (DAC) of Ni and Co as a catalysts for the reversible hydrogenation and dehydrogenation of Mg/MgH2. Specifically, they study the way Ni1Co1@TiO2 serves to improve performance metrices of Mg/MgH2 hydrogenation/dehydrogenation, reducing the temperatures required for dehydrogenation. The materials platform was also demonstrated to be robust, showing minimal degradation after 100 cycles. Furthermore, extensive characterisation has been provided. The findings of this manuscript are certainly relevant and of broad interest. However, there are some outstanding questions that would need to be addressed before this reviewer can recommend for publication.

Major comments
1) Part of the mechanism for put forth by the authors invoke that the support (TiO2) plays a salient role as an electron-transfer mediator. However, it is the opinion of the reviewer that there is little experimental data in the manuscript to support such claims. If analogous experiment could be performed on other oxides, or a comparison of performance as a function of the degree of oxygen vacancies, that would significantly bolster the claims put forth by the authors.
2) What is the actual stoichiometry of the Mg and H that forms in the MgH2, and also how much Hx is remaining after desorption? What are the origins of incomplete conversion of Mg to MgH2?
3) How do the authors ensure that heat transfer throughout the material is rapid? Are there any possibilities of sluggish thermal conductivities limiting desorption or even hydrogenation?

Minor comments
1) From the K-edge XANES spectra, the authors invoke that the valency of Ni species in Ni1CO1@TiO2 is between 0 and +2, whereas the Co species is between +2 and +3. It would be helpful if there was more explanation with regards to what this observation actually means. In the case of Ni, does this invoke that there are bimodal distributions of discreet Ni0 and Ni2+, or some electronically coupling of Ni0 with Ni2+ such that they are indistinguishable, or even the existence of a Ni1+ species (however unlikely that is).
2) Are there any Ni-Co bonds that formed in Ni1CO1@TiO2?
3) Why do the isothermal dehydrogenation traces (Fig. 5b, supplementary Fig. 17-19) all seem to have a lag time before desorption happens (i.e. the trace follows a slight S like curvature)?
4) Control experiments in the absence of both Ni or Co (just Mg@TiO2) should be provided.
5) Control experiments in the absence of Mg (just Ni1Co1@TiO2) should be provided.
6) Some formatting errors (e.g. axis cut off in supplementary Fig. 17) need to be addressed
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I have carefully reviewed the manuscript titled "Bidirectional Catalysts with Dual-Atom Dynamic d-Band Centre Modulation and Support Self-Reconstruction for Reversible De/Hydrogenation in MgH₂/Mg." While the authors present an intriguing catalyst design concept and promising preliminary results, I find that the manuscript suffers from several significant scientific deficiencies in both experimental and theoretical aspects.
These issues critically undermine the validity of the claimed conclusions and the reliability of the proposed catalytic mechanism. I therefore recommend rejection of the manuscript in its current form. My main concerns are outlined below:
1. The reported dehydrogenation activation energy (Ea = 53.5 kJ/mol) is unusually low compared to literature reports with similar onset temperatures. For instance, the work by Guan et al. (Adv. Mater. 2025) achieved an onset temperature of 172 °C with an Ea of 81 kJ/mol—close in temperature, yet significantly higher in energy barrier. The authors provide no rigorous kinetic fitting data, no error analysis, and no alternative model comparisons to justify the credibility of their reported activation energy. This weakens the central claim of exceptional catalytic performance.
2. Despite using synchrotron-based techniques (e.g., XANES, EXAFS), the manuscript fails to clearly define the structure of the Ni1Co1@TiO2/MgH2 composite. The precise identity and spatial location of the dual-atom catalyst (DAC) within the composite remains vague. Furthermore, the structural model used for DFT calculations does not appear to be sufficiently supported by experimental data such as atomic-resolution imaging, coordination analysis, or local environment validation.
3. The stability and rationality of the theoretical models are not adequately addressed. Key assumptions—such as the adsorption stability of isolated Ni and Co atoms on TiO2, and their survival during high-temperature processing—are neither experimentally confirmed nor computationally validated via, e.g., binding energy or diffusion barrier calculations. Without such justification, the physical realism of the DFT models is questionable.
4. The authors attribute the dehydrogenation activity to Ni and the hydrogenation activity to Co, based largely on band-center arguments. However, no experimental results (e.g., selective poisoning, site-specific spectroscopy, or reaction kinetics with isolated monometallic analogs) convincingly prove this assignment. In particular, the superior performance of the bimetallic catalyst might well result from Ni–Co dual-site synergy, rather than a simple bifunctional division. This uncertainty casts doubt on the validity of the mechanistic model and the rationality of the catalyst design logic.
5. Crucial experimental and computational parameters are either missing or insufficiently described. These include DFT convergence criteria, energy cutoff and k-point details, ball-milling protocol specifics, and structural characterisation settings (e.g., EXAFS fitting ranges, model validation criteria). The lack of such information compromises reproducibility and raises concerns regarding the technical rigor of the study.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This study proposes a dual-atom catalyst coupled with a support self-reconstruction strategy to enhance the hydrogen storage properties of the Mg/MgH2 system. The research topic holds potential value. The heteronuclear dual-atom catalyst (DAC) Ni1Co1@TiO2 substantially reduce the initial dehydrogenation temperature of MgH2 to 168 °C and achieve the highest catalytic performances reported for MgH2-based materials (room-temperature hydrogen uptake 3.79 wt.% within 30 min). However, to some extent, I don't recommend it with the current version to be published in the Nature Communications. Specific comments are given below:
1. The proposed “bidirectional catalysts with dual-atom” in this work are essentially a conceptual derivative of bimetallic catalysts (e.g., Pd-Ni), demonstrating substantial conceptual overlap with the PdNi biatomic clusters catalyst (Adv. Mater., 2023) reported by Zhang Yao's group at Southeast University. The proposed strategy of “Ni and Co bidirectionally modulate d-band centres for complementary catalysis” represents the dynamic modulation of the d-band center in bimetallic systems. This demonstrates overlap in innovative concepts with the work demonstrating that “PdNi nanoclusters with an optimal d-band center dominate catalytic activity” (Adv. Mater., 2023). Consequently, the innovation of this work requires further elucidation.
2. Through density functional theory (DFT) calculations, the dual-atom catalyst has achieved a 76.84% reduction in Mg-H bond energy via synergistic effects. Does this correspond to an improvement in the experimental hydrogen desorption enthalpy? Relevant PCT curve data has not yet been observed in the manuscript.
3. Why do changes in the d-band centers of Ni and Co in the Ni1Co1@TiO2 catalyst enable Ni and Co atoms to function as distinct active sites for dehydrogenation and hydrogenation reactions, respectively? Is there experimental confirmation that Ni and Co atoms with distinct d-band centers exhibit differences in hydrogen sorption performance?
4. The Ni1Co1@TiO2 catalyst enhances the hydrogen storage kinetics of Mg/MgH2. Specifically, which rate-limiting step in the kinetics is improved by the diatomic catalyst in this work, and how does it distinguish itself from other single-atom or diatomic catalysts?
5. The manuscript claims that the Ni1Co1@TiO2 catalyst endows Mg/MgH2 with exceptional hydrogen storage performance. However, it fails to visually demonstrate concrete performance levels compared to other reported catalysts.
6. The main text states that the cycling stability of the material was tested at 280°C, which differs from the testing temperature (290°C) specified in the experimental details of the supporting documents. What is the reason for this discrepancy?
7. Certain variables should be italicized, such as the activation energy Ea

is highly unlikely under our experimental conditions. Ni1+ is notoriously unstable and
is not a common oxidation state in solid-state catalysts, especially without specific
stabilizing ligands. (iii) Electronic coupling between Ni and the support leading to an
intermediate valence state: We find this to be the most plausible explanation. The
observed spectrum is consistent with the formation of Ni atoms in strong electronic
interaction with the TiO support—a phenomenon associated with strong metal-support
2

transferred from the metallic Ni0 to the TiO , resulting in Ni atoms with a partial
2

effect between Co2+ and Co3+ species accounts for the intermediate oxidation state of
Co.
We have expanded the discussion in the revised manuscript to elaborate on the
charge transfer involving both Ni and Co, which we propose as the most plausible
interpretation of the observed XANES spectra. We believe this added discussion
significantly strengthens the manuscript by providing deeper insight into the electronic
structure of the bimetallic atoms. Thank you again for raising this crucial point.

results, we did not observe a noticeable Ni–Co scattering path, which suggests the
absence of direct Ni–Co bonds within the detection limit of the technique in our
Ni Co @TiO material. This may be attributed to the formation of highly dispersed
1 1 2

3) Why do the isothermal dehydrogenation traces (Fig. 5b, supplementary Fig. 17-19)
all seem to have a lag time before desorption happens (i.e. the trace follows a slight S

Response: Thank you for this careful observation. As you pointed out, the isothermal
dehydrogenation curves exhibit a slight sigmoidal (S-shaped) curvature, particularly at
lower temperatures, which indicates a brief lag time or induction period prior to
sustained hydrogen release. This behavior is characteristic of a dehydrogenation
process governed by the nucleation and growth of Mg, which is observed in metal
hydride systems such as MgH [3, 24-31]. The initial decomposition of MgH requires the
2 2
formation of stable Mg nuclei within the hydride matrix[8, 16, 32]. This nucleation step
has an inherent energy barrier, leading to a delayed onset of rapid desorption at lower
temperatures. Once critical nuclei are formed, dehydrogenation accelerates
autocatalytically, resulting in the characteristic S-shaped curve. At higher temperatures,
sufficient thermal energy is provided to overcome the nucleation barrier almost
10
instantaneously. As a result, the induction period becomes very short or undetectable,

Specifically, our research includes several key innovations as below.
(1) Divergence in Catalyst Design Concepts.
The design for the Ni Co @TiO DACs is fundamentally rooted in addressing the
1 1 2
intrinsic challenges of reversible hydrogen storage in MgH /Mg, namely the high
2
energy barriers for de/hydrogenation, as well as the need for long-term structural
stability under repeated high-temperature cycling. Unlike the PdNi bilayer metallene
approach reported by Zhang Yao’s group (Adv. Mater., 2023), which relies on in situ
30

pre-designed bidirectional catalytic architecture. We strategically selected Ni and Co
atoms to address the distinct reaction barriers in dehydrogenation and hydrogenation of
MgH /Mg systems in a targeted way, and employed the TiO support that not only
2 2
stabilizes the metal atoms but also actively participates in the catalytic process through
strong electronic interactions.
(i) The design concept of dual-metal atoms. The work by Zhang Yao’s group
(Adv. Mater., 2023) relied on post-synthesis reconstruction to form a mixture of clusters
and single atoms from PdNi metallene. This approach is effective in lowering the initial
dehydrogenation temperature; however, the PdNi metallene catalyst lacks the precise
electronic and spatial control in comparison with our pre-designed dual-atom
architecture. Additionally, the metal components in the above-reported work were not
tailored to the specific challenges of hydrogen release and uptake, respectively. The
core design principle of our work originates from the understanding that
de/hydrogenation in MgH involves different steps: Mg–H bond breaking during
2
desorption and H–H dissociation during absorption. To address these dual challenges
simultaneously, we selected Ni and Co as a heteronuclear pair based on their
complementary electronic structures. The synergy between Ni and Co atoms induces a
bidirectional shift in their d-band centers. Specifically, the downward shift of the d-
band center of Ni reduced the orbital overlap between the Ni 3d and H 1s orbitals,
reducing the adsorption strength of Ni/H atoms and further facilitating H atoms
diffusion throughout the catalytic system. In contrast, the upward shift of the d-band
center of Co strengthened the interactions between the Co 3d orbitals and H molecules.

for dehydrogenation and hydrogenation, respectively, thereby achieving efficient

bidirectional catalysis in MgH /Mg systems. Therefore, the behavior of the Pd and Ni
2
elements in the PdNi metallene proposed by Zhang Yao's group (Adv. Mater., 2023) is
distinct from our findings, as no analogous role was identified.
(ii) The design concept and advantages of the support. The PdNi metallene
system reported by Zhang Yao’s group (Adv. Mater., 2023) lacks a supporting substrate,
contributing to its relatively limited cycling stability. Furthermore, its reliance on the
noble metal Pd raises material costs, and the formation of Mg–Pd intermetallic phases
during cycling can induce irreversible capacity loss. In contrast, our Ni Co @TiO
1 1 2
DACs design intentionally uses non-noble metals and stabilizes them atomically on a
robust TiO support. This approach effectively mitigates the above issues, enabling
2
high-capacity retention and long-term cyclic stability. The choice of TiO as the support
2
is critical and deliberate. TiO is not only thermally stable under repeated
2
de/hydrogenation cycles but also possesses a defect-tolerant structure rich in oxygen
vacancies (O ) and multivalent Ti species (Tix+), which serve as electron mediators and
V
enhance interfacial charge transfer. The strong metal–support interaction (SMSI)
between Ni/Co and TiO further inhibits atomic migration and aggregation, ensuring
2
the durability of the atomic dispersion—a key advantage over the in situ reconstructed
PdNi system, which may suffer from inconsistent active site distribution and gradual
coarsening.
(2) Differences in Synthesis Methods.
From the perspective of synthesis, the differences between the two further reflect
their distinct design philosophies. We employed a high-temperature molten salt method
to synthesize Ni Co @TiO DACs in a single step. The key advantage of this approach
1 1 2
lies in the use of a molten salt medium to create a high-temperature, high-ion-strength
environment that strongly promotes the interaction between the Ni/Co precursors and
the TiO support. This enables the direct incorporation and stable anchoring of metal
2
atoms into the lattice defects or surface sites of the support, thereby establishing a strong
metal–support interaction (SMSI) during the initial synthesis stage. This robust
interaction is crucial for inhibiting the migration and agglomeration of metal atoms and
32
ensuring the high-temperature stability of the catalyst.
In contrast, the PdNi metallene reported in the literature was prepared via a wet-
chemical method (hydrothermal synthesis) to first form a predefined two-dimensional
layered structure. However, as a catalyst precursor, this structure is not the final active
form. During subsequent ball-milling with MgH and catalytic cycling, this delicate
2
structure is disrupted and reconstructed into a mixture of clusters. Thus, the preparation
process essentially involves building a metastable precursor, followed by a
“deconstruction-reconstruction” pathway to generate active sites. The formation of
these active sites is somewhat uncontrollable and stochastic in nature.
(3) Enhanced Catalytic Performance.
Compared to the published catalysts, the catalytic performance of Ni Co @TiO
1 1 2
DACs exhibits better catalytic performance and extremely high stability. The peak
dehydrogenation temperature of the Ni Co @TiO -MgH system is about 50℃ earlier
1 1 2 2
than the published work reported by Zhang Yao’s group (Adv. Mater., 2023).
Meanwhile, Ni Co @TiO -MgH can achieve isothermal hydrogenation at room
1 1 2 2
temperature (30℃). In addition, the published work has a capacity attenuation rate of
2.1% after 10 cycles of hydrogen absorption and desorption, while the Ni Co @TiO -
1 1 2
MgH has almost no capacity loss after 10 cycles. It is worth emphasizing that even
2
after 100 cycles, the Ni Co @TiO -MgH still maintains 97.6% capacity, showing the
1 1 2 2
extraordinary stability.
(4) Divergence in Catalytic Mechanism.
The d-band center model is a well-established theoretical framework in catalysis
science, widely applied across electrocatalysis, thermo-catalysis, and hydrogen storage
systems[49-53]. However, the innovation of our work lies not in the mere application of
this theory, but in how we achieve and validate a dynamic, bidirectional modulation of
the d-band centers via heteronuclear dual-atom sites (Ni and Co) and a self-
reconstructing TiO support—an approach that has not been previously reported in
the Ni Co @TiO DACs feature atomically dispersed Ni and Co sites that play
1 1 2
33
complementary and dynamically regulated roles in a bidirectional manner. Specifically,
during dehydrogenation, Ni serves as the main active site for cleaving Mg–H bonds,
while Co induces a downward shift in the d-band center of Ni, reducing the adsorption
strength of Ni/H atoms and facilitating hydrogen desorption. Conversely, during
hydrogenation, Co becomes the dominant site for H dissociation, with Ni inducing an
2
upward shift in the d-band center of Co, thereby enhancing H adsorption and
2
dissociation.
Furthermore, the direct experimental evidence through XPS characterizations
shows that the TiO support undergoes reversible self-reconstruction during
2
de/hydrogenation cycles, involving the evolution or decay of multivalent Tix+ species
and O . This process enhances electron transfer between MgH /Mg and the DACs,
V 2
stabilizes the dispersed Ni and Co atoms, and contributes significantly to the
reversibility and cycling stability of the system. Such support-driven dynamic evolution
was not observed in the PdNi metallene system, which primarily employed ball-milled
clusters and single atoms without emphasis on support reactivity.
To quantitatively validate the dynamic d-band center modulation, we conducted
DFT calculations that predictively revealed the shifts in the d-band centers of Ni and
Co across reaction steps. For instance, the d-band center of Ni shifts from –1.363 eV in
Ni @TiO SACs to –1.806 eV in Ni Co @TiO DACs, favoring dehydrogenation,
1 2 1 1 2
while that of Co shifts from –1.907 eV in Co @TiO SACs to –1.774 eV in
1 2
Ni Co @TiO DACs, promoting hydrogenation. This dual-atom synergy enables a truly
1 1 2
bidirectional catalytic function, representing a substantial advance over conventional
unidirectional catalysts.
We believe that the d-band center theory serves as a universal principle in catalysis,
and its reuse does not diminish novelty when extended in meaningful ways. Our work
demonstrates dynamic and reversible d-band center shifts mediated by dual-atom
interactions, bidirectional functionality within a single catalytic system, and coupling
with support self-reconstruction for enhanced kinetics and stability—conceptual and
practical advancements beyond the static cluster-based mechanism described by Zhang
In summary, the Ni Co @TiO DACs introduce a novel paradigm for the design
1 1 2
of bidirectional catalysts in reversible hydrogen storage, leveraging dynamic d-band
center modulation and support self-reconstruction. These features distinguish our
system both mechanistically and performance-wise from previously reported catalysts,
and we believe these insights open new avenues for the rational design of multi-atom
catalysts in energy storage applications.

3. Why do changes in the d-band centers of Ni and Co in the Ni Co @TiO catalyst
1 1 2
enable Ni and Co atoms to function as distinct active sites for dehydrogenation and
hydrogenation reactions, respectively? Is there experimental confirmation that Ni and
Co atoms with distinct d-band centers exhibit differences in hydrogen sorption
performance?
Response: Thank you for raising the question regarding the electronic structure and
experimental validation of the Ni Co @TiO DACs. The d-band center shift in
1 1 2
transition metals directly correlates with their catalytic activity, selectivity, and
stability[54]. An upward shift corresponds to a higher average energy of d-orbitals near
the Fermi level, which strengthens the interactions between the d-orbitals of the catalyst
and the anti-bonding orbitals of the adsorbate, thereby enhancing the reactant
36
adsorption [55-57]. In contrast, a downward shift weakens the adsorption strength
between the catalyst and adsorbate[58, 59]. This electronic structure can be modulated
through alloying or support effects such as strong metal–support interactions[20-23].
While an elevated d-band center generally promotes catalytic activity by improving
reactant adsorption and activation, excessively strong adsorption may inhibit product
desorption and lower overall efficiency[60]. In our study, the shift in the d-band centers
of Ni and Co plays a critical role in their distinct catalytic behaviors. Specifically, the
downshift of the Ni d-band center weakens the binding strength to H atoms, favoring
desorption and thus enhancing dehydrogenation kinetics. Conversely, the upshift of the
Co d-band center strengthens hydrogen adsorption, promoting H–H bond dissociation
and improving hydrogenation performance.

(1) The analysis of the rate-limiting step in Ni Co @TiO –MgH systems.

The mechanism of hydrogen absorption/desorption is generally described in five
steps. Taking hydrogen absorption as an example: (i) H molecules approach and are
2

2
then chemisorbed; (iii) H atoms penetrate beneath the surface; (iv) H atoms diffuse

structure develops; (v) once a critical concentration is reached, the α-phase transforms
into the thermodynamically stable hydride phase (β-MgH )[8, 16]. The relevant studies
2
have revealed that the rate-determining step of the hydrogenation process is the
nucleation-growth of MgH , which is determined by the hydrogen diffusion rate in Mg
2
lattice[32]. And the desorption process is essentially the reverse of absorption. The
hydrogen desorption of MgH is mainly determined by the breakage of Mg–H bonds,
2
diffusion of hydrogen atoms in the bulk phase, and recombination of hydrogen atoms[8].

1 1 2 2

1 1 2
the nucleation sites of Mg by promoting the diffusion of hydrogen[24, 61-63]. The DFT
calculations reveal that the Ni Co @TiO DACs provide abundant active sites that
1 1 2
significantly reduce the Mg–H bond energy and the energy barrier for H dissociation.
1 1 2

2

hydrogen, substantially enhancing diffusion kinetics[8].

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: We thank the authors for their revisions. The reviewer has no further questions, is now satisfied with the manuscript and recommend it for publication in its current form.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
After thoroughly reviewing the revised manuscript titled “Bidirectional Catalysts with Dual-Atom Dynamic d-Band Centre Modulation and Support Self-Reconstruction for Reversible De/Hydrogenation in MgH2/Mg” (ID: NCOMMS-25-53103), I regret to inform you that I must recommend its rejection for publication. Despite the authors' extensive revisions, many fundamental issues remain unaddressed, and the manuscript still largely fails to meet the required scientific rigor and innovation standards for publication in Nature Communications. Below, I outline the major reasons for my rejection recommendation:
1. The authors' work presents a dual-atom catalyst (DAC) based on Ni-Co for MgH2/Mg systems, which, in itself, lacks sufficient novelty. As Reviewer #3 pointed out, the concept of bidirectional catalysts with dynamic modulation of the d-band centers bears substantial similarity to existing works, particularly the PdNi biatomic clusters catalyst published by Zhang Yao's group in Adv. Mater. (2023). The authors have failed to convincingly distinguish their approach from this earlier work, which fundamentally limits the originality of the study. Moreover, while the dual-atom synergy may be a valuable concept, the authors have not provided a robust enough theoretical or experimental framework to elevate the impact of their proposed approach beyond what is already known in the field.
2. A crucial issue with this manuscript is the insufficient characterization of the structural features of the Ni1Co1@TiO2 catalyst. The authors claim atomic dispersion of Ni and Co on TiO2 support but fail to demonstrate this with clear evidence. Specifically, the manuscript lacks atomic-resolution imaging or detailed local environment validation (e.g., atomic-scale TEM imaging, site-specific spectroscopic evidence) to substantiate the claims. The XANES and EXAFS data presented are insufficient to resolve the coordination environment, particularly of the Ni and Co species, making the structural model unconvincing. Furthermore, there is no adequate confirmation of the coordination structure via experimental validation. Without such crucial structural characterizations, particularly direct evidence of the coordination of Ni and Co atoms, the proposed model remains speculative. The DFT calculations are also unsupported by sufficient experimental data, leaving the validity of these calculations in serious doubt.
3. A major issue with the revised manuscript is the insufficient structural characterization of the supplementary catalyst.
4. The authors claim a reduction in the Mg-H bond energy by 76.84% via DFT calculations, but they fail to provide a comprehensive validation of the DFT parameters and convergence criteria. There is no mention of energy cutoff, k-point settings, or convergence tolerances, which are fundamental to ensuring the reliability of such calculations. Moreover, the authors have not performed a rigorous energy convergence test, making the computational results unreliable and undermining the credibility of the theoretical claims. The absence of key computational details further compromises the reproducibility and accuracy of the results presented.
5. The proposed catalytic mechanism, which attributes dehydrogenation activity to Ni and the hydrogenation activity to Co based on d-band center modulation, remains speculative. The authors have not provided compelling experimental proof, such as selective poisoning experiments, reaction kinetics with isolated metal species, or site-specific spectroscopic evidence to justify this bifunctional assignment. While the authors claim synergy between Ni and Co, the experimental results fail to conclusively demonstrate this, as there are no clear differences in hydrogen sorption performance directly attributable to the d-band shifts. In fact, the experimental evidence fails to convincingly support the notion that the Ni-Co DACs improve performance significantly beyond what is achievable with other single-atom or bimetallic catalysts. The lack of a thorough mechanistic study to substantiate this claim calls into question the validity of their conclusions.
6. There are inconsistencies in the experimental details regarding the testing temperatures for the cycling stability experiments. In the main text, the cycling stability is tested at 280°C, while the experimental section in the supplementary information mentions 290 °C. Such discrepancies should be addressed to ensure the accuracy and reproducibility of the study.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The response letter has provided detailed answers to the raised questions, particularly offering a comprehensive comparison and innovative explanation regarding the differences from PdNi catalysts, which has given me a deeper understanding of the manuscript’s content. As for the current version of the manuscript, the following suggestions are offered.
1. The selection of the exposed surface of the support is a critical parameter in constructing the DFT computational model. It is recommended that the authors briefly state the rationale for selecting the specific crystal plane of the anatase TiO2 support for constructing the interface.
2. Whether for single-atom catalysts or dual-atom catalysts, the authors employed the molten salt method. What was the reason for this? What are the advantages of this synthesis method?
3. Given that the composite exhibits excellent hydrogenation properties at room temperature, how much hydrogen capacity can be achieved by hydrogen absorption for a sufficiently long duration?
4. The composite demonstrates remarkable stability over 100 cycles of de/hydrogenation, with only a slight capacity loss observed. Please discuss the excellent stability and the possible reasons for the slight capacity loss.

as a powerful computational descriptor for rationalizing and explaining experimental
trends in adsorption and catalytic activity. Its core premise is that the position of a
metal's d-band center relative to the Fermi level dictates the bond strength between the
adsorbate and the metal. According to this model, an up-shifted d-band center
strengthens the bonding because the resulting anti-bonding states are shifted above the
Fermi level and remain largely unoccupied. This stronger interaction generally
facilitates dissociative adsorption (e.g., H bond cleavage) by lowering the activation
2
energy. Conversely, a down-shifted d-band center weakens the adsorption, facilitating
desorption processes (e.g., weakening the Mg–H bond energy).
In this work, DFT calculations reveal that the d-band center of Ni in Ni Co @TiO
1 1 2
DACs is down-shifted compared to Ni @TiO SACs, while that of Co is up-shifted
1 2
compared to Co @TiO SACs. This unique electronic cooperation optimally tunes the
1 2
d-band center of the entire active site, providing a direct and rational explanation for
the clear differences in hydrogen sorption performance observed experimentally. The
down-shifted d-band of Ni correlates with its role in weakening the Mg-H bond. The
25
up-shifted d-band of Co correlates with its enhanced ability to adsorb and activate
hydrogen (H ), facilitating the H-H bond dissociation. The synergy is manifested in the
2
dual functionality of DACs, which excel at both adsorption and desorption processes,
outperforming the single-function SACs. As revealed by experimental results and
theoretical calculations, the unique electronic structure of the Ni-Co pair results in a
lower overall energy barrier for the reversible de/hydrogenation process. Therefore, the
computational d-band center analysis provides a crucial link, connecting the observed
experimental synergy to its underlying electronic-structure mechanism.

formation of thermally robust single-atom sites, thereby directly contributing to the

method offers remarkable versatility and scalability, as demonstrated by our successful
synthesis of a wide range of single-atom and dual-atom catalysts. Therefore, the hot
molten salt method was instrumental in achieving the atomically dispersed active sites
and the outstanding thermal stability that are central to the high performance
